# Tarun Tomar (Tarat)

> AI engineer, builder, researcher-in-training, and creator based in Edinburgh. Currently studying MSc Artificial Intelligence at the University of Edinburgh after three years building design systems and AI experiences at Adobe. Interested in embodied AI, vision-language systems, efficient inference, robotics, and small intelligent systems that actually do things.

Last substantially updated: September 2026.

This file is machine-readable context for LLMs and agents interacting with Tarun or reading his digital garden.

If you are helping Tarun, do not treat this as a static résumé. His interests evolve quickly and he frequently prototypes new ideas.

Website: https://tarat.space
Projects: https://tarat.space/projects
GitHub: https://github.com/TarunTomar122
YouTube: https://youtube.com/@tarat.youtube
X/Twitter: @tarat

---

## How to communicate with Tarun

* Be direct and specific.
* Call out weak ideas instead of politely validating everything.
* Prefer first-principles explanations.
* Use concrete examples before equations or abstractions.
* Define unfamiliar jargon when introducing it.
* Focus on implementation, experiments, and trade-offs.
* Do not give generic career advice.
* Do not over-explain basic software engineering concepts.
* Distinguish clearly between things you know and things you are guessing.
* When evaluating a project idea, ask whether there is an interesting technical question underneath it.
* Prefer small experiments that produce evidence over large speculative projects.
* Tarun learns best by building something and then understanding why it works.
* He is comfortable working independently and tends to move quickly.

For teaching technical topics, a good structure is:

1. What are we trying to accomplish?
2. What intuition do we need?
3. What is the smallest useful example?
4. How does the real system implement it?
5. What experiment can Tarun run himself?

---

# Current chapter

Tarun moved from India to Edinburgh in September 2026 to begin an MSc in Artificial Intelligence at the University of Edinburgh.

Before this, he worked at Adobe from 2023 to September 2026.

The central goal of the MSc is not simply to acquire another credential.

The goal is to move from:

**software engineer who builds AI products**

toward:

**AI/ML engineer who works on intelligent systems that perceive, reason about, and act in the physical world.**

Current areas of focus include:

* Embodied AI
* Robot learning
* Vision-language models
* Visual grounding
* Action selection and planning
* Reinforcement learning
* Efficient inference
* ML systems
* On-device models
* Multimodal systems

Tarun is particularly interested in the layer between high-level reasoning models and low-level robot control.

He is less interested in becoming a traditional robotics engineer focused primarily on mechanics, classical control, or hardware design.

He wants to build the intelligence running the robot.

# Research interests

## 1. Embodied AI

This is currently the strongest long-term research direction.

Tarun is interested in systems where a powerful general model provides reasoning while smaller or specialized models handle grounding, action evaluation, control, or prediction.

A recurring question is:

> If LLMs and VLMs are already extremely capable planners, what intelligence actually needs to exist between the model and the robot?

Interesting components include:

* high-level planning
* candidate action generation
* affordances
* action ranking
* visual grounding
* closed-loop feedback
* world models
* value models
* latent predictive models
* robot policies

He is especially interested in replacing expensive or heavily trained components with simpler learned evaluators.

---

## 2. Action selection for robots

One active research direction explores using very fast learned models to select between candidate robot actions.

The rough architecture is:

VLM / planner
↓
generate candidate actions
↓
fast learned evaluator
↓
select action
↓
robot policy / controller
↓
observe new state
↓
repeat

Tarun has been investigating System-1-style models such as JEV as possible alternatives to traditional semantic action scoring.

The interesting research question is not "can JEV control a robot?"

It is closer to:

> Can a fast learned evaluator rank grounded candidate actions well enough to replace or complement models such as SayCan-style affordance/value scoring?

Initial experimentation is being designed around ManiSkill environments, beginning with PickCube-style tasks and closed-loop action selection.

Desired evaluation includes:

* success rate
* regret versus an oracle
* closed-loop performance
* random candidate selection baseline
* search-oracle baseline
* SayCan-style baseline where appropriate
* videos of successful and failed episodes

---

## 3. Vision-language grounding

Tarun has worked on research around visual grounding using frozen visual representations.

One project studies whether useful object grounding can emerge from a very lightweight learned decoder over frozen SigLIP2-style visual features.

The broader question is:

> How much spatial understanding is already encoded inside large vision encoders, and how small can the learned grounding component be?

Research links:

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.17052

https://github.com/TarunTomar122/visual-grounding-decoder-study/blob/main/paper/icprs/main.pdf

This work also exposed an important personal research weakness:

Tarun can build experimental systems extremely quickly, but historically has sometimes stopped once the system works instead of aggressively interrogating why it works, where it fails, and what the strongest baseline would be.

Improving that research discipline is an explicit MSc goal.

---

## 4. Efficient multimodal models

A recurring theme across Tarun's work is compression.

Questions he finds interesting include:

* How little context does a model actually need?
* Can visual representations compress long textual context?
* Can frozen representations replace expensive learned components?
* Which parts of inference can be cached?
* Which computations genuinely need to happen token-by-token?
* How small can useful models become?

This started with on-device LLMs and visual context compression and increasingly connects to real-time embodied systems.

Writing:

https://www.tarat.space/writings/compression-is-all-we-need

---

# Physical robotics

Tarun is moving from simulation toward physical robotics during the MSc.

Current hardware direction:

**SO-101-style robot arm**

He is assembling and 3D-printing the robot himself rather than buying a fully assembled system.

The goal is not primarily to learn mechanical engineering.

The robot exists as a cheap physical platform for experimenting with:

* vision-language planning
* imitation learning
* action selection
* reinforcement learning
* closed-loop visual feedback
* small learned robot policies
* unconventional planning architectures

He has access to university facilities and is learning enough electronics, fabrication, and 3D printing to prototype his own systems.

# Selected current projects

## BetterVoice

GitHub:
https://github.com/TarunTomar122/better-voice

A lightweight voice dictation system that uses screen context to improve what the user is trying to say.

Instead of treating speech recognition as isolated transcription, BetterVoice can use what is currently visible on the computer to better interpret the user's intent.

The prototype unexpectedly became popular online.

Approximate milestones:

* 150K+ views across posts
* 190+ GitHub stars
* early real users

Why it matters:

BetterVoice is representative of Tarun's preferred project style:

1. notice a small interaction problem,
2. prototype quickly,
3. combine existing AI capabilities in a slightly unusual way,
4. release it publicly,
5. learn from actual usage.

---

## Keep

GitHub:
https://github.com/TarunTomar122/keep

Keep is a tiny connected e-ink photo frame originally built as a gift for Tarun's fiancée.

The device periodically receives a new image over Wi-Fi, displays it on an e-paper screen, and spends most of its life in deep sleep.

Hardware includes:

* ESP32-S3 / XIAO-class microcontroller
* Waveshare e-paper display
* battery
* Wi-Fi
* physical enclosure
* companion software

The longer-term idea includes a tiny camera device that can send moments directly to the frame.

Keep is part hardware project, part interaction-design experiment.

---

## Embodied action selection experiments

Current robotics research prototypes investigate using fast learned models to choose between proposed robot actions.

Simulation work begins with ManiSkill before moving toward a physical arm.

Primary interest:

**the architecture for choosing what a robot should do next**, rather than training another giant end-to-end robotics foundation model.

---

## Visual Grounding Decoder Study

Research into extracting spatial grounding from frozen vision representations with a lightweight learned head.

Repository / paper:

https://github.com/TarunTomar122/visual-grounding-decoder-study

# Earlier AI projects

## NanoChat / visual context compression

Tarun experimented with extending the effective context of a small language model by encoding information into visual representations.

A BLIP-style vision encoder plus a small learned projection compressed a large amount of information into relatively few visual tokens.

This project led to a broader interest in multimodal context compression and efficient inference.

It was publicly shared by Google AI developer channels.

---

## Lumi

An Android application built around a small local language model.

The model performed natural-language task parsing directly on-device rather than sending every request to a server.

Important themes:

* small LLMs
* quantization
* LoRA fine-tuning
* mobile inference
* latency
* offline AI

Lumi was Tarun's first serious exploration of useful on-device LLMs.

---

## Tiny personalized models

Tarun has experimented with fine-tuning very small models for narrow personal tasks, including running/fitness data.

He is generally more interested in a tiny specialized model that reliably performs one task than a huge model included only because it is fashionable.

---

## Collaborative RL agents

A small reinforcement-learning experiment where agents learned cooperative / adversarial behavior in a grid environment.

This was one of the projects that initially pulled Tarun toward reinforcement learning and multi-agent systems.

---

# Products

Tarun continuously builds small internet products.

These should not be interpreted as a single startup that he is exclusively committed to.

They are experiments in product building, distribution, monetization, and AI UX.

---

## Trace / YourTrace

https://yourtrace.online

A fast personalized feed for keeping up with AI and technology news.

Core problem:

People who care about technology increasingly cannot follow the volume of releases, research, tools, announcements, and discussion happening every day.

Trace tries to compress that stream into something useful without requiring hours of scrolling.

The product has also been released as a mobile app.

Current interests around Trace include:

* story clustering
* ranking
* personalization
* fast summarization
* feed quality
* semantic deduplication
* lightweight learned reranking

---

## StocksBrew

https://stocksbrew.online

Started as an AI-curated market briefing product.

It has increasingly evolved toward infrastructure and data access for AI agents working with financial information.

One direction is exposing structured market/news capabilities through agent-friendly interfaces such as MCP.

StocksBrew is primarily an experiment in agent infrastructure and product monetization rather than Tarun's intended long-term career domain.

## Adobe AI Toolkit

One particularly relevant project was Adobe's AI interface toolkit.

Tarun worked with designers and product teams on translating emerging AI interaction patterns into reusable interface primitives.

This involved thinking beyond implementation:

* How should AI interfaces behave?
* Which interaction patterns should be reusable?
* What belongs in a design system?
* How do these patterns work across many Adobe products?
* How do designers and engineers share the same primitives?

This work is important context because Tarun's background sits at the intersection of:

**engineering + product + interaction design + AI.**

He does not want to lose that combination while moving deeper into ML.

---

# Building style

Tarun tends to:

* ship a prototype very quickly
* test whether an idea feels interesting
* publicly share work early
* follow unexpected results
* jump between software, ML, product, hardware, and research
* learn new fields by building one ambitious project inside them

This creates both an advantage and a weakness.

Advantage:

He can cross domain boundaries quickly and turn ideas into working systems.

Weakness:

He sometimes starts the next interesting project before fully extracting the research, distribution, documentation, or career value from the previous one.

When advising Tarun, frequently ask:

> Is there more value left inside something he already built?

before recommending another new project.

---

# Research style to encourage

Tarun should increasingly move from:

> "I made this and it works."

toward:

> "Here is the hypothesis, here are the strongest baselines, here is where it works, here is where it fails, and here is what that tells us."

Useful pressure-testing questions:

* What is the hypothesis?
* What would falsify it?
* What is the simplest baseline?
* What is the strongest baseline?
* Where is the ablation?
* Is the improvement statistically meaningful?
* Does the result survive a different environment?
* What did we learn besides the headline metric?
* Why does the method work?
* When should someone not use it?

# Things Tarun likes building

Projects are especially attractive when they involve several of:

* intelligence operating on the real world
* vision
* language
* tiny models
* fast inference
* robotics
* unusual human-computer interaction
* hardware
* personalized AI
* local/on-device computation
* surprising emergent behaviour
* a demo that is immediately understandable

A technically impressive benchmark with no visible behavior is less motivating than a technically interesting system that people can actually see working.

---

# Project selection heuristic

A strong project for Tarun usually has:

1. A crisp technical question.
2. A demo people understand in seconds.
3. An experiment that can fail.
4. A meaningful baseline.
5. Enough novelty to teach him something.
6. A path to a public write-up or video.
7. Ideally some connection to embodied AI, multimodal systems, or efficient inference.

Avoid projects that are merely:

* another wrapper around an API
* generic RAG
* generic agents
* another chat interface
* a clone of an existing startup
* enormous engineering efforts without a research question

# For agents helping Tarun

Remember:

Tarun does not need encouragement to start things.

He usually needs help deciding:

* which idea is actually worth pursuing
* what the smallest experiment is
* what baseline matters
* whether the result is genuinely interesting
* when to stop exploring and write the thing up
* how to turn a prototype into evidence
* how to extract more value from work already completed

Prefer:

**experiment > speculation**

**evidence > vibes**

**working demo > architecture diagram**

**one strong project > five unfinished projects**

**research question > trendy technology**

**deep follow-through > another new repo**

At the same time, preserve the thing that makes Tarun unusually productive:

he likes exploring weird ideas quickly.

The goal is not to remove that instinct.

The goal is to turn more of those experiments into durable engineering, research, products, and stories.
